steps.label: Instruction Sets
steps.content:
3.1 Computer Architecture

Instruction Sets

Year 10

  • Today: about 20 minutes of notes. Then use your notes in Bridge Builder.
  • The big question: why can a program made for one CPU fail on another CPU?
  • One small memory all lesson: address 6 holds 12, address 7 holds 30.
Think → Pair → ShareA game made for a games console will not run on a laptop, even when the files are copied across. Why might that be?Show the answer

Collect ideas: the two computers are built differently inside. Today shows one big reason, inside the CPU.

steps.label: Why a CPU Has a Fixed List
steps.content:
Why a CPU Has a Fixed List

This CPU has circuits for:
CodeCommand
0001LOAD
0010ADD
0011SUB
0100STORE
0101OUTPUT
  • The CU and the ALU have circuits for these five commands.
  • They have no circuit for any other command.

A program asks for MULTIPLY

It is not in the list. The CPU cannot process it.

Instruction set: the list of all the commands that can be processed by a CPU.

WHY? A CPU can only do what its circuits were built for. To multiply, a program must use ADD again and again.

steps.label: Your Notes: The Instruction Set
steps.content:
Your Notes: The Instruction Set

What to do: open your notes (the pen icon at the top). Write the heading and the note below. You will use these notes in Bridge Builder.

Instruction set
A list of all the commands that can be processed by a CPU.
WHY a CPU can only process its own commands
Its CU and ALU have circuits for only those commands. Any other command cannot be processed.

steps.label: Why Instructions Are Binary
steps.content:
Why Instructions Are Binary

  • A program is stored in memory, just like data.
  • Memory can only store 0s and 1s.

What we write

LOAD 6

What memory stores

0001 0110
  • LOAD is 0001: the instruction set gives each command its own binary code.
  • 6 is 0110 (4 + 2).
Machine code: instructions in binary, using the codes in the instruction set.

WHY? Memory is made of tiny switches, on or off. It cannot store the word LOAD.

What to do: open your notes (the pen icon at the top). Write the heading and the note below. You will use these notes in Bridge Builder.

Machine code
Instructions in binary, using the codes in the instruction set.
WHY programs are stored as machine code
Memory can only store 0s and 1s.
Example
LOAD 6 is stored as 0001 0110.

steps.label: Two Parts: Opcode and Operand
steps.content:
Two Parts: Opcode and Operand

  • Each instruction is 8 bits: two parts of 4 bits.
0010 0111
Opcode (first 4 bits): says which command. 0010 is ADD.
Operand (last 4 bits): says what to use, such as an address. 0111 is 7 (4 + 2 + 1).

WHY? The CPU needs two things: what to do, and what to do it with.

steps.label: Watch: Decoding 0010 0111
steps.content:
Watch: Decoding 0010 0111

Think → Pair → ShareBefore you watch: the CU has only 0s and 1s. How could it work out what to do?Show the answer

Ideas: split it into parts, look the parts up, turn binary into a number. Watch to check.

steps.label: Decoding: Two Examples
steps.content:
Decoding: Two Examples

The instruction set
OpcodeCommand
0001LOAD
0010ADD
0011SUB
0100STORE
0101OUTPUT
0010 0111
  1. Split: 0010 | 0111
  2. Look up 0010: ADD
  3. Convert 0111: 7
  4. ADD 7: ACC 12 + 30 = 42
0001 1001
  1. Split: 0001 | 1001
  2. Look up 0001: LOAD
  3. Convert 1001: 9 (8 + 1)
  4. LOAD 9: copy address 9 into the ACC
Decode: the CU splits the instruction, then looks up the opcode in the instruction set.

WHY? The instruction is only 0s and 1s. The instruction set tells the CU which command each opcode means.

steps.label: Your Notes: Opcode, Operand and Decoding
steps.content:
Your Notes: Opcode, Operand and Decoding

What to do: open your notes (the pen icon at the top). Write the heading and the note below. You will use these notes in Bridge Builder.

Opcode and operand
Opcode: the part that says which command. Operand: the part that says what to use, such as an address.
How to decode
Split into opcode and operand. Look up the opcode in the instruction set. Convert the operand to a number. Example: 0010 0111 is ADD 7.
WHY the CU needs the instruction set
The instruction is only 0s and 1s. The instruction set tells the CU which command each opcode means.

steps.label: Two CPU Types, One Program
steps.content:
Two CPU Types, One Program

  • A program is made for CPU A. Its first instruction is 0001 0110.
CPU A
OpcodeCommand
0001LOAD
0010ADD
0011SUB
0100STORE
0101OUTPUT

0001 is LOAD: it runs LOAD 6. Correct.

CPU B
OpcodeCommand
0001OUTPUT
0010LOAD
0011ADD
0100STORE

0001 is OUTPUT: it runs OUTPUT. Wrong job. 0101 is not in its list at all.

WHY? Each CPU decodes with its own instruction set. The same machine code means a different command, or nothing.

steps.label: Your Notes: Different CPU Types
steps.content:
Your Notes: Different CPU Types

What to do: open your notes (the pen icon at the top). Write the heading and the note below. You will use these notes in Bridge Builder.

WHY machine code for one CPU may not run on another
The other CPU decodes with its own instruction set. The same opcode can mean a different command, or nothing.
Which CPUs can run a machine code program
Only CPUs with the same instruction set as the one it was made for.
